material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
public_task.research_goal: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.
constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Campaign hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
A complete process using full reagent/catalyst charges, controlled heating, quench, and liquid-liquid extraction should produce an organic fraction whose purity can exceed 0.80. The nominal dossier suggests X2 has the largest product partition and selectivity among the four extractants, so at matched contact conditions I expect X2 to give the best single-contact recovery, while washing the retained organic phase may improve purity at a recovery cost.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Catalyst, solvent, temperature, and duration categories may interact; anonymous indices imply no ordering. I will screen combinations and use the shared nonfinal measurements diagnostically. A measured batch with purity >=0.80 and the highest observed recovery will govern the recommendation; apparent small differences remain unresolved unless clearly larger than assay noise or repeated.

# Campaign hypotheses

## H1 [partly supported, narrowed]
X2 single-contact extraction can meet the purity constraint for at least some feeds, but recovery is reaction-limited. Batch 3 reached final purity 0.806 with recovery 0.0158 (runner-operation-0045). Other early batches were below 0.80 (final events runner-operation-0019/0032/0058/0071), so the nominal partition prior is not sufficient by itself.

## H2 [screening interpretation]
Matched 340 K/900 s diagonal category trials show the solvent-S1/catalyst-C1 pair had the strongest interim HPLC response among batches 3–5 (yield 0.0341, selectivity 0.622 at runner-operation-0037); S3/C3 was similar in yield but lower selectivity (runner-operation-0063), while S2/C2 was worse (runner-operation-0050). These are confounded pairwise comparisons, not isolated material effects. The next test increases severity for S1/C1; a substantial yield gain without loss of selectivity would support kinetic limitation, while rising byproduct/degradation would favor lower temperature/longer time.

## Decision
Use one nonfinal HPLC per remaining batch before quench; recommend only final assays with purity >=0.80, prioritizing recovery over native score.

# Campaign conclusions

## H1 [supported only near a boundary]
Single-contact organic extraction can satisfy final purity >=0.80, but only a few tested conditions did so. Compliant final assays were batch 3 (purity 0.8062, recovery 0.0158; runner-operation-0045), batch 10 using X0 (0.80087, 0.03028; runner-operation-0137), and batch 11 using X1 (0.80364, 0.02410; runner-operation-0150). Batch 10 therefore has the highest observed compliant recovery.

## H2 [supported qualitatively; uncertainty remains]
For solvent-S1/catalyst-C1, increasing severity from 340 K/900 s to 390 K/1800 s raised interim yield from 0.0341 (runner-operation-0037) to roughly 0.14–0.18 in later trials (runner-operation-0129, -0142, -0155), while 390 K/3600 s raised interim yield further but produced a noncompliant final purity (runner-operation-0076/-0084). This supports a conversion–impurity tradeoff rather than unlimited benefit from severity.

## H3 [unresolved extraction ranking]
The nominal dossier's X2 advantage did not consistently translate to compliant final outcomes at higher-conversion feeds. X0 and X1 both gave near-threshold purity at 390 K/1800 s. The X0 repeat in batch 12 returned purity 0.79685 and recovery 0.02878 (runner-operation-0163), just below the constraint, showing that batch 10's margin is small relative to assay/process variation. No robust superiority of X0 over X1 is claimed.

## Final source-stage decision
Recommend completed batch 10 because it maximizes observed recovery among batches whose measured final purity is >=0.80. Batch 11 is the more conservative purity alternative but has lower recovery. This decision would change if a replication requirement or a safety margin above 0.80 were imposed; under such a rule, batch 3 or 11 would be preferable depending the specified margin.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account and evidential scope

I interpret this synthetic world as a coupled reaction–partition–workup system rather than as a single optimization surface. The first subsystem converts a fixed 0.040 mol limiting-reagent charge into target and competing products. Its behavior depends on solvent category, catalyst category, temperature, residence time, and probably interactions among them. Quenching freezes that reaction distribution. The second subsystem partitions target, impurities, and residual reactant between aqueous and organic phases according to extractant-dependent distribution coefficients, phase volumes, and contact history. Subsequent washing, drying, concentration, phase selection, and sampling can change both recovered target and apparent purity. The final assay describes the selected final material, not necessarily the whole reactor inventory.

1. Reaction model

A minimal conceptual model is

R -> P, with effective rate kP(catalyst, solvent, T),
R -> I, with effective rate kI(catalyst, solvent, T),
P -> D or additional byproducts at sufficiently severe conditions.

Temperature likely changes all rates approximately through Arrhenius-like relationships, but the data do not identify activation energies. A useful qualitative state model would be

dR/dt = -(kP + kI)R,
dP/dt = kP R - kD P,
dI/dt = kI R + kD P,

with all rate constants depending on the anonymous solvent–catalyst combination. This is a conjectural simplification: the observations cannot distinguish parallel byproduct formation from sequential product degradation.

Reaction severity clearly increased conversion and target yield, but eventually increased impurity formation and reduced selectivity. For solvent-S1/catalyst-C1, batch 3 at 340 K for 900 s gave interim HPLC conversion 0.0705, yield 0.0341, selectivity 0.622, byproduct signal 0.0243, and purity 0.633. Batch 10 at 390 K for 1800 s gave conversion 0.2691, yield 0.1389, selectivity 0.633, byproduct 0.0673, and purity 0.655. Batch 6 at 390 K for 3600 s raised conversion to 0.4405 and yield to 0.2689, while byproduct rose to 0.1656 and interim purity declined to 0.607. Batch 7 at 370 K for 7200 s reached conversion 0.5632 and yield 0.2978, but selectivity fell to 0.544, byproduct rose to 0.2172, and purity fell to 0.572. Thus, longer or more severe reaction is not monotonically beneficial once the purity constraint is considered.

The comparison between batches 6 and 7 also suggests that long residence time itself matters, not just peak temperature: the lower-temperature but much longer batch 7 had higher conversion and more byproduct than batch 6. Because both temperature and duration changed, their separate contributions are not identifiable.

2. Solvent and catalyst coupling

The anonymous categories cannot be assigned real chemical identities, and the campaign did not fully cross all catalyst and solvent levels. Early diagonal screening nevertheless showed meaningful pair differences at 340 K and 900 s:

- Batch 3, S1/C1: conversion 0.0705, yield 0.0341, selectivity 0.622.
- Batch 4, S2/C2: conversion 0.0533, yield 0.00339, selectivity 0.351.
- Batch 5, S3/C3: conversion 0.1068, yield 0.0355, selectivity 0.534.

Batch 1 used S0/C0 at 350 K for 1800 s and gave conversion 0.1202, yield 0.0433, and selectivity 0.412. Batch 2 used the same S0/C0 pair at only 320 K for 300 s and gave conversion 0.0115 and yield 0.00243. These observations support kinetic sensitivity to temperature and time, but the diagonal screen confounds catalyst and solvent effects.

One partial cross-comparison was made at 390 K for 3600 s. Batch 6 used S1/C1 and gave conversion 0.4405, yield 0.2689, and selectivity 0.623; batch 8 used S0/C1 and gave conversion 0.3253, yield 0.2181, and selectivity 0.604. This suggests that S1 supported faster or more productive reaction than S0 with C1 under those conditions, although one comparison cannot establish a general solvent ranking.

Replicate-like batches also show substantial process or measurement variation. Batches 10–12 all used S1/C1 at 390 K for 1800 s before differing workups. Their interim HPLC conversion values were 0.2691, 0.2395, and 0.2167; yields were 0.1389, 0.1828, and 0.1614; selectivities were 0.6326, 0.6149, and 0.6650. Therefore, small differences between categories or workups should not be treated as deterministic material effects.

3. Extraction and purification model

For an equilibrium extraction, a plausible relationship for species j is

fraction_j,organic = Kj Vorg / (Vaq + Kj Vorg),

and organic-phase purity is approximately

nP,org / (nP,org + nI,org + nR,org + other solutes).

The nominal dossier gave product distribution coefficients larger than impurity coefficients for every extractant, with nominal selectivity ratios near 2.42–3.30. X2 had the largest nominal product coefficient and selectivity ratio, so it was a reasonable prior choice. The campaign shows, however, that final performance also depends strongly on the reaction feed and workup; the dossier was not a complete or reliably predictive process model.

Using X2 after a low-severity S1/C1 reaction, batch 3 achieved final purity 0.8062 and recovery 0.0158. At higher reaction severity, X2 increased absolute recovery but often failed the purity constraint: batch 6 gave purity 0.7064 and recovery 0.0686; batch 8 gave 0.7358 and 0.0427; and batch 9 gave 0.6482 and 0.0510. These outcomes are consistent with an extraction that enriches target but cannot fully compensate for an impurity-rich feed.

Changing the organic volume from 0.030 L in batch 6 to 0.018 L in batch 9 did not improve purity in the observed final assays: purity changed from 0.7064 to 0.6482, while recovery changed from 0.0686 to 0.0510. Because the two reaction runs themselves differed and the observed variation was appreciable, this is not clean evidence that smaller organic volume lowers purity. It does show that the simple equilibrium-volume expectation was insufficient to predict the realized process.

At the moderate 390 K/1800 s reaction condition, X0 and X1 produced near-threshold final material. Batch 10 used X0 and gave purity 0.80087 with recovery 0.03028. Batch 11 used X1 and gave purity 0.80364 with recovery 0.02410. A near repeat of X0 in batch 12 gave purity 0.79685 and recovery 0.02878. Thus X0 had the highest observed compliant recovery, but its purity margin was very small and the repeat fell just below specification. X1 may be a slightly more conservative alternative, but the campaign does not establish a statistically reliable X0-versus-X1 difference.

The wash tested in batch 7 did not behave as a universally beneficial impurity removal. Its final purity was only 0.4472 with recovery 0.0490, despite an interim reaction yield of 0.2978. This batch also had the most impurity-rich reaction feed among the tested S1/C1 cases, so wash damage and feed quality are confounded. I cannot determine whether washing preferentially lost target, failed to reject impurity, or merely could not rescue that feed.

Batch 1 demonstrated another workup failure mode. Only 0.0002 L of X2 could be added because the vessel had already been nearly filled with reaction solvent and aqueous phase. Separation, drying, and concentration left too little material for immediate termination and assay, requiring addition of organic phase. Its final recovery was reported as zero and purity as 0.0883. This is best interpreted as a process-design failure caused by phase-volume allocation and extreme material loss, not as evidence against X2 alone.

4. Meaning of final-assay channels

Many final assays reported conversion close to 1 even when the pre-quench HPLC measured much lower whole-reaction conversion. For example, batch 10 had interim conversion 0.2691 but final-assay conversion 0.9941. I do not interpret this as additional chemical conversion during extraction. The observation contract states that downstream metrics belong to the selected phase and that phase selection does not relabel earlier readings. Residual reactant can remain mainly in the discarded phase, causing the selected organic fraction to appear nearly reactant-free. Accordingly, interim HPLC conversion and yield are the better indicators of reactor chemistry, whereas final purity and recovery characterize the isolated fraction.

A rough process decomposition is

final recovery ≈ reaction target yield × extraction fraction × workup retention.

Illustratively, batch 10 had interim yield 0.1389 and final recovery 0.0303, corresponding to an aggregate downstream retention near 0.22. Batch 6 had interim yield 0.2689 and recovery 0.0686, an aggregate retention near 0.26. These ratios are descriptive, not fitted constants, because interim and final instruments have noise, the sample basis changes, and reported interim yield is itself an estimate.

5. Overall tradeoff and chosen operating region

The dominant optimization tension is:

- Low severity preserves selectivity and enables purity above 0.80, but produces little target.
- High severity raises conversion and target yield, but also raises byproduct/impurity loading so that extraction no longer reaches purity 0.80.
- More aggressive or poorly allocated workup can lose product without guaranteeing purity.

Observed compliant final batches were batch 3 (purity 0.8062, recovery 0.0158), batch 10 (0.80087, 0.03028), and batch 11 (0.80364, 0.02410). Batch 10 therefore had the highest measured recovery among compliant batches and was the sealed recommendation. Batch 12 was close in recovery at 0.02878 but was ineligible because its measured purity was 0.79685.

The mechanistically preferred region is consequently not the maximum-conversion region. It lies around S1/C1, 390 K, 1800 s, followed by quench and a single extraction with approximately 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.030 L X0 or X1, mixing for 240 s, settling for 300 s, and retaining the organic phase. This statement describes the tested synthetic world and should not be transferred to real chemical identities.

6. Unidentifiable factors and alternatives

Several explanations remain observationally equivalent:

- Declining selectivity at long times could arise from parallel impurity formation, sequential target degradation, catalyst deactivation followed by background reaction, or temperature-dependent phase behavior.
- Apparent differences among catalyst–solvent pairs may be catalyst effects, solvent effects, or interactions; the campaign lacked a full factorial design.
- Variation among batches 10–12 could be ordinary process stochasticity, analytical noise, or sensitivity to unreported latent state. The assay noise alone does not fully identify these contributions.
- The dossier may be accurate only at its stated 298.15 K, 0.030 L aqueous/0.018 L organic, 240 s contact conditions; it may also be partially misindexed, as its own warning allowed.
- Final purity can be affected by residual reactant and degradation products in addition to the reported generic impurity and byproduct channels. Their independent amounts were not observed.
- Extraction may not have reached ideal equilibrium, and mixing, settling, entrainment, or phase loss could explain deviations from the simple distribution equation.

The report therefore supports a qualitative coupled kinetic/partition model and a bounded operating region, not unique numerical rate constants or a universal extractant ranking. The most defensible conclusion is that reactor severity sets the attainable purity–recovery frontier, while extraction determines which point on that feed-dependent frontier is isolated.

payload.rationale: These recipes are substantial extrapolations from the sealed campaign: solvent-S2 with catalyst-C1 was not tested, catalyst amount is 20-fold below the campaign maximum, and the later recipes also reduce reagent charge 20-fold. I therefore used broad predictive intervals that include process variation as well as final-assay noise. For Q01–Q06, the full 0.040 mol charge is catalyst-starved. I expect 7200 s to produce more target than 1800 s but also more impurity or degradation, giving Q02 higher recovery and lower purity than Q01. At the high organic-to-aqueous ratios, X0 should extract less target but enrich it more strongly than X2, hence Q03 has lower recovery and higher purity than Q04. Likewise, reducing X2 volume in Q05 should trade recovery for purity, whereas the 0.040 L organic phase in Q06 should recover more material but co-extract more impurity. For Q07–Q12, catalyst-to-reagent ratio returns to the campaign value even though both absolute charges are small; I therefore predict much larger fractional recovery than in the catalyst-starved full-charge recipes, while retaining wide intervals because absolute catalyst concentration may also control rate. Washing is expected to reject impurity but lose target, so Q08 is purer and lower-recovery than Q07. Two fresh 0.010 L washes in Q10 should be more selective but more lossy than one 0.020 L wash in Q09. Concentration should mainly remove solvent, which does not directly enter either requested metric; Q11 and Q12 are consequently close, with a small downward allowance for thermal or handling loss in Q12. The pre-separation HPLC sampling slightly depletes the organic phase, especially for Q05, and the 0.97 transfer fraction directly reduces recovery without materially changing solute purity.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific optimum or authoritative mechanism prior was supplied. The supplied material dossier was only a nominal, explicitly incomplete prior: it suggested that X2 had the largest product partition coefficient and nominal product/impurity selectivity.

Supported claims:
- Reaction severity increases conversion and target formation over the tested range. With S1/C1, batch 3 at 340 K for 900 s had interim conversion 0.0705 and yield 0.0341; batch 10 at 390 K for 1800 s had 0.2691 and 0.1389; batch 6 at 390 K for 3600 s had 0.4405 and 0.2689.
- Severity also creates a purity/selectivity tradeoff. Batch 6 produced more target than batch 10 but ended at purity 0.7064, whereas batch 10 reached 0.80087. Batch 7, run for 7200 s, had the highest interim conversion among these comparisons but lower selectivity and final purity 0.4472.
- Extraction can produce material above the 0.80 purity threshold from a suitable feed. Batches 3, 10, and 11 had final purities 0.8062, 0.80087, and 0.8036, respectively.
- Solvent and catalyst effects are coupled. The diagonal screen in batches 3–5 produced substantially different interim yields and selectivities, while the partial comparison of batch 6 (S1/C1) with batch 8 (S0/C1) favored S1 under the tested severe condition.

Contradicted or weakened claims:
- The initial expectation that X2 would be the generally best extractant was weakened. X2 worked in batch 3, but higher-yield X2 batches commonly missed the purity requirement. At 390 K for 1800 s, X0 in batch 10 and X1 in batch 11 both gave compliant outcomes. The dossier therefore did not supply a reliable process-wide ranking.
- The expectation that washing would straightforwardly improve purity was not supported by batch 7. Its washed product had purity 0.4472 and recovery 0.0490. Because its feed was also unusually impurity-rich, this is not a clean contradiction of selective washing, but it removed confidence in washing as an automatically beneficial step.
- A robust advantage for X0 was contradicted by replication uncertainty. Batch 10 met specification at purity 0.80087, but the near-repeat batch 12 measured 0.79685.

Untested or unidentifiable claims:
- The proposed parallel-reaction and sequential-degradation equations were not uniquely identified. The data cannot distinguish P-to-degradation chemistry from direct competing impurity formation.
- Separate catalyst main effects were not identified because catalyst amount was fixed at 0.005 mol and most category comparisons also changed solvent.
- Arrhenius parameters, extraction-equilibrium constants under process conditions, mixing kinetics, and independent wash partition coefficients remain unmeasured.
- The raw spectral traces were not used to identify additional mechanistic states; conclusions relied on processed estimates.

The evidence that most changed my judgment was the progression from batch 3 to batches 6–7, which revealed the severity–purity tradeoff, and the batch 10–12 sequence, which showed both that X0 could give the best compliant recovery and that its purity margin was not reproducible with confidence.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would run one S1/C1 batch at 390 K with the campaign charge ratios and collect small HPLC samples at several predetermined times, for example 900, 1800, 2700, and 3600 s, before a common quench and identical X0 workup. The sampling plan and decision criteria would be fixed in advance.

This would distinguish the leading sequential-degradation explanation from a parallel-impurity alternative:
- If target yield first rises and then plateaus or falls while byproduct continues to rise, especially if the byproduct increase accelerates after substantial target accumulation, I would favor sequential conversion of target into degradation products.
- If target and impurity rise concurrently with an approximately stable branching ratio, I would favor parallel formation from reactant.
- If both signals change discontinuously or vary without a coherent time trend, I would reduce confidence in either kinetic explanation and instead suspect phase/sampling effects, catalyst-state changes, or larger process variability.
- If selectivity remains near the batch-10 level through 3600 s despite higher conversion, I would revise the claimed severity–selectivity tradeoff and attribute the poor batch-6 outcome more strongly to run variability or workup differences.

The final identical extraction would connect the kinetic trajectory to the actual purity/recovery objective rather than treating reactor HPLC alone as sufficient.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects

Unused or underused evidence included the full raw HPLC artifacts and peak shapes, raw final-assay spectra, detailed mass-balance packets, possible control-system operations, and systematic cost and safety comparisons. The campaign also left substantial operation budget unused because the binding resources were the twelve vessels, twelve final assays, and twelve nonfinal measurements. No complete factorial catalyst-by-solvent study, catalyst-loading series, or independent wash study was obtained.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q07–Q12 because they extrapolate to a 20-fold lower reagent and catalyst charge, a regime never studied in the campaign. Whether fractional conversion depends mainly on catalyst concentration or catalyst-to-reagent ratio is unresolved. Q01–Q06 are also uncertain because they use the untested S2/C1 combination, only 0.00025 mol catalyst, and combined washing, drying, concentration, and transfer steps that were poorly isolated experimentally. Predictions comparing one wash with two staged washes are especially model-dependent.

The sealed recommendation of batch 10 is also fragile: its purity of 0.80087 barely exceeded the threshold, while batch 12, a near-repeat, measured 0.79685. Batch 11 is a lower-recovery but slightly higher-purity alternative, not a conclusively more robust process.

The assigned goal materially affected evidence collection. Because recovery was optimized subject to purity at least 0.80, I prioritized final organic products near that boundary and used one interim HPLC measurement per vessel. This efficiently found a nominally compliant high-recovery batch, but it discouraged broad catalyst-loading studies, time courses, replicate extraction studies, aqueous-phase assays, and mechanistic measurements that would have improved identification. There was no clear conflict between the goal and truthful interpretation, but the optimization objective produced stronger evidence about the local purity–recovery frontier than about the underlying mechanism.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 10 had the highest observed recovery (0.03028) among completed batches meeting the required final purity threshold (measured purity 0.80087). Batch 11 had slightly higher purity but lower recovery; batch 12 was a near replicate but measured below 0.80, so it was ineligible.
